The Egyptian Ministry’s overview dates the Predynastic period to about 5500–3100 BCE.
Nile Valley communities developed distinct regional cultures before Egyptian political unification.
The ministry places Badarian culture around 5500–4000 BCE near modern Asyut.
The Maadi cultural complex developed near modern Cairo around 4000–3100 BCE.
Naqada I is dated around 4000–3500 BCE in Upper Egypt.
The ministry describes increasing social differentiation towards the period’s end.
The Met dates the Old Kingdom to approximately 2649–2130 BCE.
Much of the surviving evidence for material culture comes from funerary contexts.
Djoser’s reign is dated approximately 2649–2630 BCE in this chronology.
His Saqqara funerary complex included Egypt’s first pyramid.
The Met places Khufu’s reign around 2551–2528 BCE.
Khufu’s Great Pyramid at Giza was built as his tomb and is the largest Egyptian pyramid.
The New Kingdom is dated approximately 1550–1070 BCE.
Theban royal tombs and mortuary temples supported elaborate funerary traditions.
A settlement in western Thebes housed artists who made royal tombs.
Around 3200 BCE, Uruk was a major city in southern Mesopotamia.
Clay pictographs recorded goods and workers’ rations, preceding later cuneiform.
The Met dates the Early Dynastic period to 2900–2350 BCE.
City rulers acquired luxury materials through trade and conquest.
The Met dates the flourishing urban Indus civilization to approximately 2600–1900 BCE.
Harappa and Mohenjo Daro were large settlements connected with western trading partners.
Seals preserve writing that remains undeciphered.
The Shang dynasty is dated approximately 1600–1046 BCE.
Its political centre lay along the Yellow River in present-day Henan.
The Western Zhou period is dated 1046–771 BCE.
Zhou rulers exercised authority across much of central China.
The Eastern Zhou period is dated 770–256 BCE.
After the capital moved to Luoyang, regional states became increasingly autonomous.
The Western Han period lasted from 206 BCE to 9 CE.
Chang’an was its capital, with palaces, residential wards and market areas.
The Eastern Han period lasted from 25 to 220 CE.
Its capital was Luoyang; diplomacy and long-distance exchange expanded.
Emperor Wu ruled during 141–87 BCE.
His reign promoted Confucian learning in official conduct and education.
Olmec cultural and artistic activity flourished around 1200–400 BCE in Veracruz and Tabasco.
Sculptors used imported volcanic stone and jade.
After about 900 BCE, La Venta developed platforms and a major pyramid.
Monumental building and carving there ceased after about 400 BCE.
UNESCO reports Caral’s development between approximately 3000 and 1800 BCE.
Its architecture includes large platform mounds and sunken circular courts.
UNESCO’s reference position places Caral in Peru’s Supe Valley.
UNESCO describes Kush as a major power from the eighth century BCE to the fourth century CE.
The Meroe region preserves royal, religious, domestic and water-management remains.
Khufu succeeded his father Snefru in the Fourth Dynasty. Snefru commissioned three large pyramids and developed the smooth-sided pyramid form.

Fourth Dynasty pyramid complexes included temples and a causeway. State-planned cemeteries for officials surrounded Khufu’s pyramid, and senior officials were often relatives of the king in a highly centralised administration.
UNESCO places the northern Japanese sequence represented by these sites at approximately 13,000–400 BCE.
Settled communities relied on hunting, fishing and gathering; their sites preserve dwellings, graves, earthworks and stone circles.
The official site guide dates the settlement at Sannai Maruyama to approximately 3900–2200 BCE.
At Aomori, planned dwellings, storage pits and roads accompanied a diet evidenced by nuts, fish and animal remains; imported materials included jade and obsidian.
UNESCO dates the dolmen tombs at Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa broadly to the first millennium BCE.
These cemeteries preserve hundreds of tombs assembled from large stone slabs.
The Dilmun burial mounds in western Bahrain were built approximately 2200–1750 BCE.
Bahrain’s role as a trading centre supported elaborate burial traditions, preserved in extensive mound fields and royal tombs.
The Met’s chronology places Lapita settlement of Island Melanesia and western Polynesia around 1500–500 BCE.
Communities expanded eastward across the western Pacific and made distinctively decorated pottery.
The Met dates the emergence of Arnhem Land’s X-ray rock-art style to around 2000 BCE and describes it as continuing to the present.
Artists depicted internal organs and bones within human and animal figures.
UNESCO dates the Chavín cultural context in this Peruvian highland valley to approximately 1500–300 BCE.
Its place of worship includes terraces, plazas and dressed-stone structures with animal-like ornament.
The map uses UNESCO’s reference position for Chavín’s ceremonial landscape, not a territorial boundary.
The National Park Service dates residential and ceremonial use of Poverty Point to approximately 1700–1100 BCE.
Hunter-fisher-gatherers built monumental earthworks in the Lower Mississippi Valley and participated in far-reaching exchange networks.
The map uses UNESCO’s reference position for Poverty Point’s mound builders, not a territorial boundary.
UNESCO places Sammallahdenmäki in the Scandinavian Bronze Age context of approximately 1500–500 BCE.
Communities built granite burial cairns in clusters along a ridge in western Finland.
The map uses UNESCO’s reference position for Sammallahdenmäki’s burial cairns, not a territorial boundary.
UNESCO describes the monumental city’s building period broadly as the first through seventh centuries CE.
Large pyramids and temples formed part of a city laid out according to geometric and symbolic principles.
The map uses UNESCO’s reference position for Teotihuacán’s monumental city, not a territorial boundary.
The Met places Villanovan culture approximately between 900 and 500 BCE and identifies it as a predecessor of Etruscan culture.
The Met describes an identifiable Etruscan language around 700 BCE and cultural flourishing through the end of the second century BCE.
Metal-rich Etruria supported skilled bronze workers whose products circulated around the Mediterranean.
The Met dates the Parthian imperial era to 247 BCE–224 CE.
Trade supported patronage of sculpture, metalwork, jewellery and ceramics, combining Hellenistic and earlier Near Eastern traditions.
The Met gives Mithridates I’s reign as approximately 171–138 BCE.
The Met dates settlement at Jenne-jeno to the third century BCE, with its archaeological sequence beginning around 250 BCE.
The settlement occupied the fertile Middle Niger floodplain in what is now Mali.
UNESCO describes the Aksumite kingdom in northern Ethiopia across the first to eighth centuries CE.
Its exchange networks linked inland northeastern Africa with the Red Sea through the port of Adulis.
The map uses UNESCO’s reference position for Aksum and Red Sea exchange, not a territorial boundary.
UNESCO identifies Sanchi as a major Buddhist sanctuary from the third century BCE through the first century CE.
Ashoka’s pillar and a brick stupa were followed by enlargement and ornamentation under later dynasties.
The map uses UNESCO’s reference position for Early Buddhist Sanchi, not a territorial boundary.
The Met describes Scythian migration to the northern Black Sea region in the late eighth century BCE and substantial replacement by Sarmatian groups by the late second century BCE.
Politically diverse pastoral horse-riding communities traded and interacted with neighbouring Greek settlements.
The ministry dates this period to approximately 3100 BCE–2686 BCE.
The first two dynasties followed the formation of a united Egyptian kingdom.
The ministry dates this period to approximately 2181 BCE–2055 BCE.
Provincial governors gained independence as central royal control weakened.
The ministry dates this period to approximately 2055 BCE–1650 BCE.

The ministry dates this period to approximately 1650 BCE–1550 BCE.
Hyksos power in the northeastern Delta coexisted with Egyptian rulers farther south.
The ministry dates this period to approximately 1069 BCE–747 BCE.
Kings based at Tanis shared power with increasingly autonomous authorities in Upper Egypt.
The ministry dates this period to approximately 747 BCE–332 BCE.
Kushite, Saite and Persian phases form part of this broad period of changing rule.
The ministry dates this period to approximately 332 BCE–30 BCE.
Alexander’s conquest was followed by rule under Ptolemy and his successors.
The ministry dates this period to approximately 30 BCE–395 CE.
Egypt became a Roman province; agriculture and production served the imperial economy.

The city was an important centre for the worship of Ptah.
Thebes was a capital in the Middle and New Kingdoms and a major centre of Amun worship.
The ministry dates Amenhotep IV/Akhenaten’s rule to approximately 1352–1336 BCE.
The king promoted Aten worship and founded a new capital, Akhetaten, in Middle Egypt.
At Deir el-Medina in western Thebes, a community of artists and craftspeople created royal tombs and left evidence of everyday life.

Stonehenge developed over many generations. The first earthwork was built around 3000 BCE; the main stone settings followed around 2500 BCE. The early monument was also a burial place. Later changes included rearranging the bluestones and creating the Avenue towards the River Avon.
The map marks the archaeological site, using the Heritage Gateway reference coordinates.
Around 3000 BCE, people built a circular ditch and banks at Stonehenge. Cremated remains were buried within and around the monument.
The map marks the archaeological site, using the Heritage Gateway reference coordinates.
Around 2500 BCE, builders erected the large sarsens and smaller bluestones at the centre of Stonehenge.
The map marks the archaeological site, using the Heritage Gateway reference coordinates.
Bluestones were rearranged and the Avenue was built around 2300–2200 BCE. The Y and Z pits date to around 1800–1500 BCE. These were separate episodes, not continuous building work.
The map marks the archaeological site, using the Heritage Gateway reference coordinates.
Ubaid villages and towns: approximately 5500–4000 BCE.
Ubaid communities used irrigation and fishing; some villages grew into towns centred on monumental buildings, including Eridu and Uruk.
Mesopotamia’s Uruk period: approximately 4000–3100 BCE.
Cities developed around monumental mud-brick temples; administrative practices changed with writing on clay and the use of cylinder seals.
Building Avebury: approximately 2850–2200 BCE.
Avebury includes banks, ditches and stone circles; the precise sequence of construction remains incompletely understood.
Village life at Skara Brae: approximately 3100–2500 BCE.
Skara Brae’s stone houses preserve hearths, beds and storage furniture. The inhabitants farmed, hunted and fished and made tools, pottery and jewellery.
Building Newgrange and the Boyne tombs: approximately 3200 BCE.
Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth are prehistoric passage tombs in Brú na Bóinne, whose carved stones preserve megalithic art.
Yangshao communities: approximately 5000–3000 BCE.
The National Museum of China lists Yangshao painted pottery, stone knives and mortar, spindle whorls and bone needles.
Liangzhu’s city and waterworks: approximately 3300–2300 BCE.
Liangzhu combined rice cultivation, urban planning, earthen monuments and water management. Differences in burials express social hierarchy.
Malta’s megalithic temples: approximately 4000–2001 BCE.
Malta and Gozo’s temple complexes combine upright slabs and horizontal stonework, often approached through forecourts; plans and decoration vary.
Communities before the kingdom of Kerma: approximately 3500–2500 BCE.
Pre-Kerma settlement included a large enclosure, interpreted as protection for people and wealth. Evidence for wider Upper Nubian connections remains limited.
The kingdom of Kerma: approximately 2500–1500 BCE.
Kerma was the centre of a Nubian kingdom south of Egypt, near the Nile’s Third Cataract. Its capital and eastern cemetery preserve evidence spanning roughly 2500–1500 BCE.
Early cultivation at Kuk: approximately 5000–4490 BCE.
At Kuk in the New Guinea highlands, people cultivated plants on raised mounds along wetland margins. Research dates this phase to about 5000–4490 BCE and identifies intensive banana cultivation.
Ditched cultivation at Kuk: approximately 2400–2030 BCE.
Later farmers at Kuk used ditches to cultivate wet ground. The research dates the beginning of this phase to about 2400–2030 BCE.
Watson Brake’s mound builders: approximately 3500–2800 BCE.
Watson Brake has eleven mounds and connecting ridges. Building was episodic. Food remains include nuts, fish and deer and indicate broad-spectrum foraging.

Julius Caesar lived from 100 to 44 BCE, during the final decades of the Roman Republic. His rise ended in dictatorship and assassination. His death did not restore political stability. His heir Octavian, later known as Augustus, eventually emerged as Rome’s first emperor. The connections below follow the people and conflicts that link Caesar’s lifetime to that change.

Cleopatra VII lived from 69 to 30 BCE and was the last queen of the Ptolemaic dynasty. Her position joined the politics of Egypt to the struggles for power in Rome. Her relationships with Caesar and then Mark Antony were also political alliances. In Egypt, she drew on established traditions of royal authority while adapting them to her own circumstances.
Pompey lived from 106 to 48 BCE. He first worked with Caesar in a political alliance, then fought against him in civil war. Defeat at Pharsalus drove him to Egypt, where he was killed.

Cicero was a Roman politician, lawyer and philosophical writer. His speeches and letters give us a particularly close view of the Republic’s final decades. As consul in 63 BCE, he suppressed Catiline’s conspiracy. He later watched the struggle between Caesar and Pompey turn into civil war. Caesar’s assassination brought only a brief respite: Cicero was killed on Mark Antony’s orders in 43 BCE.

Mark Antony fought for Caesar and became one of the central figures in the struggle after his death. He and Octavian were allies before becoming rivals. His alliance with Cleopatra tied his future to Ptolemaic Egypt. Octavian defeated their forces at Actium in 31 BCE. Antony died the following year.

Born in 63 BCE, Octavian became Caesar’s heir after the assassination in 44 BCE. He was still a young man when he entered the struggle for power that followed. Victory over Antony and Cleopatra at Actium removed his principal rivals. In 27 BCE, the Senate granted him the title Augustus. He died in 14 CE; his lifespan and his years as emperor are shown separately.

Cleopatra ruled Egypt from 51 to 30 BCE. She belonged to the dynasty established by Ptolemy I, one of Alexander’s successors. Her reign brought that long history into direct contact with Caesar, Antony and Octavian. The links here lead back into Ptolemaic Egypt and forward to Roman rule.
Caesar became consul in 59 BCE with the support of Pompey and Crassus. The alliance helped secure his command in Gaul after his year in office.

Caesar campaigned in Gaul from 58 to 50 BCE. During these years, his armies also crossed the Channel into Britain. The two British expeditions belong within this wider series of campaigns. They did not establish lasting Roman occupation of Britain.

Caesar crossed to Britain twice, in 55 and 54 BCE. The second expedition was the larger attack, directed against communities in the south-east. His troops withdrew. Diplomatic and trading relationships continued across the Channel, but permanent Roman occupation came much later.
In 49 BCE, Caesar led his army across the Rubicon into Italy. This crossing began open civil war with Pompey and his allies.
Caesar defeated Pompey at Pharsalus in 48 BCE. Pompey escaped to Egypt. Caesar followed, bringing the Roman conflict into the struggle over Egypt’s throne.
Caesar arrived in Alexandria in 48 BCE and supported Cleopatra’s claim to the throne. Fighting kept him in Egypt into 47 BCE. He left Cleopatra in power, supported by Roman troops.

Caesar was assassinated on 15 March 44 BCE. His concentration of power had made the survival of republican government a central issue. His death opened another struggle for control. Octavian, his heir, eventually became Augustus.
On 2 September 31 BCE, Octavian defeated the forces of Antony and Cleopatra at Actium. Follow their connections to see how this Roman conflict also became the final crisis of Ptolemaic Egypt.

Roman rule began in Egypt in 30 BCE, after Cleopatra’s death. The Ptolemaic dynasty, established by Ptolemy I in 305 BCE, had ended. This is the point where the Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt entries meet. It marks a change in government, not an end to Egyptian society or its traditions.

In 27 BCE, the Senate granted Octavian the title Augustus. This entry follows his rule from that settlement to his death in 14 CE. His separate life entry begins in 63 BCE, allowing you to compare his age with Caesar, Cleopatra and Antony.

In the first century BCE, elaborate stone gateways were added to the Great Stupa at Sanchi. The Archaeological Survey of India associates this work with the Andhra-Satavahanas. The carvings tell stories from the Buddha’s life and the Jatakas. Alongside the wars around the Mediterranean, the timeline shows a community investing in a Buddhist sanctuary with a much longer history.

Alcibiades was an Athenian politician and commander whose career crossed the divisions of the Peloponnesian War. Brought up under Pericles’ guardianship, he became closely associated with Socrates. He helped persuade Athens to send its great expedition to Sicily, then fled to Sparta after being recalled for trial. His later return to Athenian service makes his life a useful way through the war’s changing alliances.

Pericles was an Athenian politician and commander, born around 495 BCE. His career belonged to the period when Athens became a dominant power in the Greek world. He was still leading the city at the beginning of the Peloponnesian War. He died during the epidemic in 429 BCE, early in a conflict that would continue for another quarter of a century.

Nicias was an Athenian commander and politician who favoured peace with Sparta. The treaty negotiated in 421 BCE bears his name. He opposed the proposed expedition to Sicily but nevertheless became one of its commanders alongside Alcibiades and Lamachus. His career ended with the expedition’s defeat in 413 BCE.

Sparta led the coalition fighting Athens in the Peloponnesian War. Its victory in 404 BCE forced Athens to give up its empire. Alcibiades’ connection takes you inside that rivalry: after leaving Athenian service, he sought refuge with the Spartans and advised them against his own city.
Getty city reference for Sparta, not Spartan territory

Syracuse was the principal target of the Athenian expedition to Sicily. Its defenders, aided by the Spartan commander Gylippus, resisted the siege. The Athenian expedition was destroyed in 413 BCE. Syracuse’s connections show this part of the war from the city being attacked, rather than only from Athens.
UNESCO Ortygia reference for Syracuse, not a siege position

The Peloponnesian War set Athens and its allies against Sparta and its coalition. It ran from 431 to 404 BCE, with a negotiated peace interrupting the main conflict. Fighting extended well beyond the two cities. The Sicilian expedition and Persian involvement are part of the same history. Athens eventually surrendered and lost its empire.

A severe epidemic struck Athens during the early years of the war. People had crowded into the city for protection, and the disease killed soldiers and civilians, including Pericles in 429 BCE. Thucydides survived it and described what he saw. The illness is conventionally called the plague of Athens, but its precise cause remains uncertain.
Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location

Socrates and Alcibiades were deployed to Potidaea in 432 BCE. Socrates served as a hoplite, an infantry soldier. The episode places their relationship in military service as well as philosophical conversation.

Socrates fought at Delium in 424 BCE, when the Athenian army was defeated. Plato’s dialogues later present Alcibiades and Laches praising his conduct during the retreat. These are literary accounts of the event, not transcripts made on the battlefield.

Athens and Sparta agreed to peace in 421 BCE after ten years of war. Nicias was closely associated with the negotiations. The settlement did not resolve the rivalries between the cities and their allies. The later Sicilian expedition and renewed war show how limited the peace proved.

Athens sent a major expedition to Sicily in 415 BCE. Alcibiades, Nicias and Lamachus shared the initial command. Alcibiades was recalled, and the remaining commanders pursued the campaign against Syracuse. Despite reinforcements, the expedition ended in disaster in 413 BCE. Many survivors became prisoners.
UNESCO Ortygia reference for Syracuse, not a siege position

Just before the fleet sailed for Sicily, sacred stone figures called herms were mutilated across Athens. The attack provoked an investigation into sacrilege. Alcibiades became caught up in accusations concerning religious offences. Accusations against him should not be read as proof that he personally damaged the herms.
Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location

Recalled from Sicily for trial in 415 BCE, Alcibiades escaped to Sparta. He advised Athens’ enemies as the war widened. By 412 BCE he was helping Spartan operations in Ionia. This was a changing political allegiance, not an uninterrupted stay in the city of Sparta.
Getty city reference for Sparta, not Spartan territory

An oligarchic coup replaced Athenian democracy with the government of the Four Hundred in 411 BCE. Hopes of obtaining Persian support formed part of the political manoeuvring. Alcibiades was involved in proposals linking a change of government to his own return. The new regime was divided from the start.
Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location
Alcibiades returned to Athens in 407 BCE after years away from the city. His return belongs to the war’s final phase. It did not end the conflict, which continued until Athens’ defeat in 404 BCE.
Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location

After the naval victory at Arginusae in 406 BCE, Athens prosecuted the commanders over the failure to recover men and bodies from the sea. Socrates opposed the unlawful collective proceedings. Six generals were executed.
Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location
Lysander defeated the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BCE. The defeat was followed by the siege of Athens. The city surrendered the following year.

Athens surrendered in 404 BCE, ending the Peloponnesian War. Its Long Walls were demolished. Peace did not immediately restore political stability. The government of the Thirty and a civil conflict followed.
Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location

After Athens’ defeat, an oligarchic government known as the Thirty took power with Spartan backing. Opposition to its rule developed into civil war. The regime was short-lived. Democratic forces recovered ground, and a settlement in 403 BCE restored democracy.
Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location

A settlement in 403 BCE restored Athenian democracy after the rule of the Thirty and the fighting that followed. The Spartan king Pausanias intervened in the reconciliation. Socrates’ trial belongs to this restored democracy, four years later. The two events should not be collapsed into one.
Acropolis reference for Athens, not the exact event location

Darius II ruled the Persian Empire during the later years of the Peloponnesian War. His officials negotiated with Sparta, and Persian money helped support its fleet. This places the war within a wider struggle over influence in the Aegean and western Anatolia. Persia was an active participant, not just a distant background.

Around 404 BCE, Amyrtaeus established himself as an Egyptian ruler and began consolidating independence from Persia. He was the sole king of the Twenty-eighth Dynasty. The change did not happen everywhere at once. Documents from Elephantine still recognised the Persian king as late as 401 BCE. This is a gradual political transition, despite the single date on the timeline.

The Mauryan dynasty brought much of the Indian subcontinent under one ruling house. Chandragupta founded it, followed by Bindusara and Ashoka. Its capital was Pataliputra. The connections here follow the rulers, their dealings with Alexander’s successors and the surviving evidence of Ashoka’s reign.
The Mauryan Empire: 321 BCE to 185 BCE. Approximate dynastic chronology follows the Met’s main text, 321–185 BCE; its heading uses 323. No fixed territorial border is implied.

Chandragupta took power in Magadha and established the Mauryan dynasty. His expansion connected the Ganges valley with the north-west, where Alexander’s successors were competing for control. He reached a settlement with Seleucus. Bindusara succeeded him; the date of that succession is approximate.
Chandragupta Maurya’s reign: 321 BCE to 297 BCE. Reign, not lifespan. Uses Livius’s conventional 321–c.297 BCE chronology. Early Mauryan chronology is debated.

Bindusara succeeded his father Chandragupta and was followed by his son Ashoka. His reign sits between two better documented rulers. Accounts attribute expansion in central India to him, but some assign the same conquests to Ashoka. The division is uncertain.
Bindusara’s reign: 297 BCE to 272 BCE. Approximate reign, not lifespan, following Livius. Other chronologies place the succession to Ashoka differently.

Ashoka was the third Mauryan emperor. He supported Buddhism and had inscriptions placed across his empire. These surviving texts make his rule unusually visible. They let us compare what a king said about government and conduct with the monuments and places connected to his reign.
Ashoka’s reign: 273 BCE to 232 BCE. Reign, not lifespan. The Met uses c.273–232 BCE; Livius gives accession in 272. Accession and coronation chronologies differ. No birth date is inferred.

Ashoka used inscriptions on rock and polished stone pillars to communicate beyond his court. They recorded royal instructions and ideas about conduct. The surviving inscriptions are evidence of particular statements in particular places, rather than proof that every subject lived by the same rules.

Ashoka’s rock and pillar inscriptions: 254 BCE to 232 BCE. Editorial window from the Met’s starting date of 254 BCE to the end of Ashoka’s reign. Not a continuous carving programme or the date of every edict.

Seleucus served under Alexander and later established a kingdom of his own. He sought refuge with Ptolemy in Egypt before recovering power in Babylonia. His settlement with Chandragupta connects the struggles among Alexander’s successors with the rise of the Mauryan state. He was assassinated in 281 BCE.
Seleucus I Nicator: 358 BCE to 281 BCE. Approximate birth c.358 BCE; death 281 BCE. Lifespan, not reign. No continuous personal itinerary is inferred.

Chandragupta and Seleucus reached a settlement after conflict near the Indus. Their agreement connected the Mauryan state with one of the kingdoms formed after Alexander’s death. The early evidence does not clearly establish who won the fighting. Later accounts have turned that uncertainty into very different stories.

Chandragupta and Seleucus make peace: 305 BCE to 303 BCE. One episode within approximately 305–303 BCE, following Jansari’s publisher synopsis. This range does not establish three years of uninterrupted warfare or a precise treaty date.

Pataliputra was the Mauryan capital. The Greek envoy Megasthenes described a city defended by a timber wall, gates and towers. That account gives us a view of the capital through a visitor’s writing. It should not be treated as a complete description of everyday life there.

Pataliputra under the Mauryas: 321 BCE to 185 BCE. Editorial window follows the dynasty, not the foundation or end of the city. Megasthenes’ description is literary testimony. A precise map reference has not yet been checked.

Lumbini is a Buddhist pilgrimage site in what is now southern Nepal. Its archaeological remains include Ashoka’s inscribed pillar and structures dating back to the third century BCE. The pillar connects the place to a recorded royal visit, alongside the longer history of worship at the site.

Lumbini: 300 BCE to 201 BCE. Third-century BCE study window, not the lifespan of the site. UNESCO’s traditional date for the Buddha’s birth is not used here. The point is the World Heritage property reference.

Ashoka visited Lumbini and erected an inscribed pillar there. UNESCO dates the pillar to 249 BCE. This is a dated connection between a ruler and a place, rather than a general assumption that he visited every site associated with his dynasty.
Ashoka’s visit to Lumbini: 249 BCE to 249 BCE. Year follows UNESCO. The map uses the property reference, not a reconstructed route.

Taxila preserves several successive settlements. The Bhir mound contains the remains of an early historic town; Sirkap and Sirsukh belong to later phases. Its position brought it into contact with Persia, the Greek world and Central Asia. Buddhist monasteries and monuments were part of its changing urban landscape.
Taxila: 500 BCE to 200 CE. 500 BCE–200 CE is an editorial window within a much longer history. The point marks Bhir Mound, one component of the UNESCO property, not all Taxila or a political border.

Alexander entered Taxila in 326 BCE. UNESCO associates this episode with the Bhir mound, the earliest historic settlement in the archaeological complex. The city’s history extends beyond that encounter. Its other entries and connections put the campaign alongside the region’s urban and religious history.
Alexander enters Taxila: 326 BCE to 326 BCE. Year follows UNESCO. The point is the Bhir Mound site reference, not an exact camp or route.

Ying Zheng conquered the remaining rival states and became the First Emperor. His government imposed common systems of writing, money and measurement. His burial complex, with its terracotta army, gives a different view of the resources his rule could command.
Qin Shi Huang: 259 BCE to 210 BCE. Lifespan follows the Met. The point associated with his death is his tomb, not a location for every year of his life.

Qin’s conquests brought the competing states under one emperor. Officials administered the new empire through commanderies and prefectures. The dynasty was short-lived, but its administrative arrangements influenced later governments.
The Qin Empire: 221 BCE to 206 BCE. Dynastic period, distinct from the earlier state of Qin. No fixed territorial outline is implied.
In 221 BCE, Qin’s conquests established a unified empire under the First Emperor. This marks a change in government across the conquered states, rather than the beginning of Chinese history.
Qin unifies the competing states: 221 BCE to 221 BCE. Year follows UNESCO. Unification refers to the contemporary competing states, not the borders of modern China.

Work on the First Emperor’s burial complex began in 246 BCE. Its layout echoed the capital, Xianyang. The tomb mound, surrounding pits and terracotta army formed parts of a much larger funerary landscape near present-day Xi’an.
The First Emperor’s mausoleum: 246 BCE to 210 BCE. Construction study window ends with the emperor’s death. It does not date every feature or imply the site ceased to exist.

The First Emperor’s burial complex contained thousands of clay soldiers and horses, alongside weapons and bronze chariots. Their surviving details provide evidence of military equipment and the work of potters and metalworkers.
Making the terracotta army: 246 BCE to 210 BCE. Broad mausoleum construction window, not independently established start and finish dates for the statues. The point marks the army pits.

Chang’an was the Western Han capital. Palaces, residential districts and markets occupied a city organised along a north–south axis. It provides an urban setting for the dynasty’s rulers, writers and trade.

Chang’an under the Western Han: 206 BCE to 9 CE. Western Han study window, not foundation dates or an assertion that it was the capital from the first year. Precise geographic reference not yet checked.

Sima Qian’s Shiji became a model for later Chinese histories. It also described peoples beyond the empire’s borders. Those descriptions preserve the historian’s perspective as well as information about the people he discussed.
Sima Qian’s Historical Records: 141 BCE to 87 BCE. Editorial window uses Emperor Wu’s reign. These are not the start and completion dates of the work or Sima Qian’s lifespan.
Ban Chao was a Han general from a literary family. Between 73 and 94 CE he reasserted Han control in Central Asia. His career connects the Eastern Han with the routes and communities to its west.
Ban Chao: 32 CE to 102 CE. Lifespan follows the Met. The campaign range does not supply a year-by-year itinerary.

The Eastern Han ruled from Luoyang, east of the earlier capital at Chang’an. Two large palace complexes dominated the city. Caravans and visiting envoys connected the capital with places beyond the empire.
Luoyang under the Eastern Han: 25 CE to 220 CE. Eastern Han study window, not the foundation or end of the city. Precise geographic reference not yet checked.

Octavia was Augustus’ sister and married Mark Antony. She tried to mediate between the two men as their alliance deteriorated. After Antony’s death, she brought up children from his marriages and his relationship with Cleopatra alongside her own family. Her household became part of the dynasty Augustus was building.
Octavia the Younger: 69 BCE to 11 BCE. Approximate lifespan. The plotted dates follow Livius’s 69 BCE birth and use 11 BCE from its alternative death dates of 11 or 10 BCE.

Livia married the future Augustus in 38 BCE and became an important adviser. Her son Tiberius eventually succeeded him. She continued to exercise influence after Augustus’ death. Hostile stories about her role in the family’s deaths should not be treated as established fact.
Livia Drusilla: 58 BCE to 29 CE. Lifespan follows Store norske leksikon: 58 BCE–29 CE. Dates are at year resolution; there is no year zero. No continuous personal location is inferred.

Ban Zhao was a scholar and teacher at the Eastern Han court. She helped complete the history of the Western Han after her brother Ban Gu died. Her writing also addressed women’s education and conduct. It gives us a named woman’s argument about family life, rather than a neutral account of how every household worked.
Ban Zhao: 48 CE to 116 CE. Approximate lifespan follows Columbia: c.48–c.116 CE. Pang-White’s Cambridge summary gives c.45–117. These are uncertain endpoints, not exact ages.

Plutarch describes Octavia arriving in Athens with money, clothing and soldiers for Antony. He told her to remain there. This records a particular journey in the breakdown of their marriage and political alliance. It does not provide a complete itinerary.

Octavia brings support to Athens: 35 BCE to 35 BCE. The Loeb edition’s footnote dates the arrival to 35 BCE. The map uses the Acropolis to locate Athens, not to claim that Octavia visited that monument.

Livia married Octavian, the future Augustus, in 38 BCE after her divorce from Tiberius Claudius Nero. Their marriage joined the family of her sons Tiberius and Drusus with the man who would become Rome’s first emperor.
Livia marries the future Augustus: 38 BCE to 38 BCE. Year follows Store norske leksikon. No wedding location is assigned.

Ban Zhao’s Lessons for Women discussed education, marriage and conduct. It combined an argument for women’s learning with expectations of obedience within the household. Read as advice, the text reveals the standards its author wanted women to follow. It cannot tell us how all women actually lived.
Ban Zhao’s Lessons for Women: 100 CE to 100 CE. Approximately 100 CE, following Pang-White’s public chapter summary. The single plotted year is an approximate date, not an exact publication year.
Acropolis reference within Athens; not evidence of a visit to the monument.

Pompeii’s excavated streets bring houses, shops, baths and theatres into the same view. They let us follow activities that often disappear behind accounts of emperors and wars. The eruption of Vesuvius buried the city in 79 CE. Its remains preserve evidence from different phases of the city’s life, not a record of every inhabitant.
Pompeii: 1 CE to 79 CE. 1–79 CE is an editorial window for the early imperial city, not its foundation date. The map uses UNESCO’s Pompeii component reference.

A house at Pompeii was converted into a fullery, where workers washed clothes and processed cloth. Vats occupied the former domestic spaces, and a terrace was used for drying. The archaeological park describes most of the workforce as enslaved. The building connects household architecture with demanding commercial labour.

Washing clothes at Pompeii: 79 CE to 79 CE. Snapshot of evidence preserved by the 79 CE eruption, not a one-year business or its opening date. Stephanus’s ownership is inferred from inscriptions; the identity of a body found at the entrance is not assumed. Map point locates Pompeii, not the individual workshop.

At the shop associated with Vetutius Placidus, customers could buy hot food and drinks from a masonry counter fitted with large jars. The house behind it was connected to the business. A shrine on the back wall included household protectors and the gods Mercury and Dionysus. Commerce, domestic space and religious practice met in one building.

Food, trade and a household at Pompeii: 79 CE to 79 CE. Evidence preserved in 79 CE, not the shop’s founding year or full operating period. The map uses the city reference rather than an unchecked shop coordinate.

The eruption of Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in 79 CE. Their remains preserve buildings, objects and traces of work and domestic life. The linked entries explore some of that evidence, alongside people living elsewhere at the time.
Vesuvius buries Pompeii and Herculaneum: 79 CE to 79 CE. Year-level event. No exact day or month is adopted. The map locates Pompeii as one affected city, not the volcano or the full disaster area.

A limestone writing surface from Deir el-Medina lists forty workers and records reasons for absence. They include illness, deaths in the family, house building and work for a superior. This was an administrative record, not a survey of everyone’s working life. It gives individual glimpses of the obligations and interruptions behind the royal tombs.

Why Egypt’s tomb workers missed work: 1279 BCE to 1213 BCE. Shown within Ramesses II’s reign. The museum description assigns the register to his Year 40, while its catalogue metadata gives c.1250 BCE. The discrepancy is unresolved; this broad window does not mean the register spans the reign.
